source_text: Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ Δαυῒδ παρανομοῦντα λαβὼν τὸν Σαοὺλ, καὶ φόνου πνέοντα, καὶ μυρίας ὄντα κολάσεως ἄξιον, οὐ μόνον αὐτοῦ τῆς ζωῆς ἐφείσατο, ἀλλ' οὔτε ῥῆμα φορτικὸν εἰς αὐτὸν ἐκβαλεῖν ὑπέμεινε· καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν τίθησι λέγων, ὅτι Χριστὸς Κυρίου ἐστίν. Οὐκ ἐντεῦθεν δὲ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἑτέρωθεν ἐκ πολλῆς τῆς περιουσίας ἔστιν ἰδεῖν, πῶς πόῤῥω που τὰ τῶν ἱερέων διορθοῦν τὸν ἀρχόμενον ἑστηκέναι χρή. Τῆς γὰρ κιβωτοῦ ποτε ἀναγομένης, ἐπειδή τινες τῶν ἀρχομένων περιτρεπομένην καὶ καταπίπτειν μέλλουσαν ἰδόντες ἀνώρθωσαν, ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ χωρίῳ δίκην ἔδοσαν, ὑπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου πληγέντες καὶ νεκροὶ μείναντες. Καίτοι γε οὐδὲν ἄτοπον ἐποίουν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀνέτρεπον τὴν κιβωτὸν, ἀλλ' ἀνατρέπεσθαι μέλλουσαν καὶ καταπίπτειν ἀνώρθουν. Ἀλλ' ἵνα ἐκ πολλῆς περιουσίας μάθῃς τῶν ἱερέων τὸ ἀξίωμα, καὶ πῶς οὐ θέμις τὸν ὑποτεταγμένον καὶ ἐν τάξει λαϊκῶν ὄντα τοιαῦτα ἐπανορθοῦν, ἀπέκτεινεν αὐτοὺς ἐν μέσῳ τῷ πλήθει, τοὺς ἄλλους πάντας ἐκ πολλῆς φοβῶν τῆς ὑπερβολῆς, καὶ πείθων μηδέποτε τοῖς τῆς ἱερωσύνης προσιέναι ἀδύτοις. Εἰ γὰρ δὴ μέλλοιεν ἕκαστοι ἐπὶ προφάσει τοῦ τὰ κακῶς γινόμενα διορθοῦν εἰς τὸ τῆς ἱερωσύνης εἰσάγειν ἑαυτοὺς ἀξίωμα, οὔτε πρόφασις ἐπιλείψει διορθώσεώς ποτε, οὔτε ἄρχοντα, οὔτε ἀρχόμενον διαγνωσόμεθα, ἀναμεμιγμένων πάντων ἀλλήλοις. Καὶ μή μέ τις νομίσῃ τῶν ἱερέων κατεγνωκότα ταῦτα λέγειν (διὰ γὰρ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ χάριν, πολλὴν, ὡς καὶ ὑμεῖς ἴστε, τὴν ἐπιείκειαν ἐν ἅπασιν ἐπιδείκνυνται, καὶ οὐδεμίαν οὐδενί ποτε παρεσχήκασι λαβὴν), ἀλλ' ἵνα ὑμεῖς μάθητε, ὅτι εἰ καὶ μοχθηροὺς εἴχετε πατέρας καὶ φορτικοὺς διδασκάλους, οὐδὲ οὕτως ἀκίνδυνον ὑμῖν ἦν, οὐδὲ ἀσφαλὲς βλασφημεῖν αὐτοὺς καὶ λοιδορεῖσθαι. Εἰ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῶν σωματικῶν γονέων σοφός τίς φησι, Κἂν ἀπολίπῃ σύνεσιν, συγγνώμην ἔχε· τί γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἀποδώσεις, καθὼς αὐτοί σοι; πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τῶν πνευματικῶν τοῦτον φυλάττεσθαι χρὴ τὸν νόμον, καὶ τὸν ἑκάστου βίον ἑαυτὸν ἕκαστον περιεργάζεσθαι καὶ πολυπραγμονεῖν, ἵνα μὴ ἀκούσωμεν κατ' ἐκείνην τὴν ἡμέραν, Ὑποκριτὰ, τί βλέπεις τὸ κάρφος τὸ ἐν τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου, τὴν δὲ ἐν τῷ σῷ ὀφθαλμῷ οὐ κατανοεῖς δοκόν; Καὶ γὰρ ὑποκριτῶν ἔργον, τὸ δημοσίᾳ μὲν καὶ πάντων ὁρώντων τὰς χεῖρας φιλεῖν τῶν ἱερέων, καὶ γονάτων ἅπτεσθαι, καὶ παρακαλεῖν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν εὔχεσθαι, καὶ δεομένους βαπτίσματος ἐπὶ τὰς ἐκείνων τρέχειν θύρας, οἴκοι δὲ καὶ ἐν ἀγοραῖς τοὺς τοσούτων ἀγαθῶν αἰτίους ἡμῖν καὶ διακόνους μυρίοις πλύνειν ὀνείδεσιν, ἢ ἑτέρων ὀνειδιζόντων ἀνέχεσθαι. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἀληθῶς κακὸς ὁ πατὴρ, πῶς αὐτὸν ἀξιόπιστον εἶναι νομίζεις διάκονον τῆς τῶν φρικτῶν ἐκείνων μυσταγωγίας; Εἰ δὲ ἀξιόπιστος ἐκείνων εἶναί σοι δοκεῖ διάκονος, τίνος ἕνεκεν ἀνέχῃ κακῶς ἑτέρων λεγόντων αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐκ ἐπιστομίζεις, οὐδὲ ἀγανακτεῖς, οὐδὲ δυσχεραίνεις, ἵνα παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ πολὺν τὸν μισθὸν ἀπολάβῃς, καὶ παρ' αὐτῶν ἐκείνων τῶν κατηγορούντων τὸν ἔπαινον; Κἂν γὰρ μυριάκις ὦσιν ὑβρισταὶ, πάντως ἐπαινέσονταί σε καὶ ἀποδέξονται τῆς περὶ τοὺς πατέρας κηδεμονίας· ὥσπερ, ἂν μὴ τοῦτο ποιῶμεν, ἅπαντες ἡμῶν καταγνώσονται, καὶ αὐτοὶ οἱ κακῶς λέγοντες. Καὶ οὐ τοῦτο μόνον ἐστὶ τὸ δεινὸν, ἀλλ' ὅτι καὶ ἐκεῖ τὴν ἐσχάτην δώσομεν δίκην.
thought_title: The honor due to priests, even unworthy ones
orientation: Chrysostom is continuing his warning against slandering spiritual fathers, now giving Old Testament examples of the danger of correcting or dishonoring priests.
pass_a_gloss: For this reason also David, having taken Saul who was acting lawlessly, and breathing murder, and being worthy of ten thousand punishments, not only spared his life, but did not even endure to cast a harsh word at him; and he gives the reason, saying, that he is the Lord's anointed. And not from this alone, but also from another side, from great abundance it is possible to see how far the affairs of the priests must stand from correcting the one under authority. For when the ark was once being brought up, since some of those under authority, seeing it being overturned and about to fall, set it upright, in that very place they paid the penalty, having been struck by the Lord and having remained dead. And yet they were doing nothing improper; for they were not overturning the ark, but they were setting upright one about to be overturned and to fall. But in order that you might learn from great abundance the dignity of the priests, and how it is not lawful for the one who is subject and in the rank of the laity to correct such things, he killed them in the midst of the multitude, frightening all the others from great excess, and persuading them never to approach the sanctuaries of the priesthood. For if each one were going to bring himself into the dignity of the priesthood on the pretext of correcting things done badly, neither will a pretext for correction ever be lacking, nor will we distinguish ruler or ruled, all things being mixed up with one another. And let no one think that I say these things having condemned the priests (for through the grace of God, they display great gentleness in all things, as you also know, and have never given any handle to anyone), but in order that you may learn, that even if you had wicked fathers and burdensome teachers, not even so was it without danger for you, nor safe, to blaspheme them and revile them. For if concerning bodily parents a certain wise man says, Even if he loses understanding, have forbearance; for what will you give back to them, as they to you? much more concerning spiritual parents must this law be guarded, and each one must busy himself with and examine his own life, in order that we may not hear on that day, Hypocrite, why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but you do not perceive the beam in your own eye? For indeed it is the work of hypocrites, in public and while all are watching to kiss the hands of the priests, and to touch their knees, and to ask them to pray for them, and when in need of baptism to run to their doors, but at home and in the marketplaces to wash with ten thousand reproaches those who are the causes and ministers of so many good things for us, or to tolerate others reproaching them. For if the father is truly bad, how do you consider him a trustworthy minister of those awesome mysteries? But if he seems to you a trustworthy minister of those things, for what reason do you tolerate others speaking badly of him, and do you not silence them, nor become angry, nor show displeasure, in order that you may receive a great reward from God, and praise from those very accusers? For even if they are ten thousand times insolent, they will altogether praise you and accept your care for the fathers; just as, if we do not do this, all will condemn us, even those very ones who speak badly. And this is not the only terrible thing, but that also there we will pay the extreme penalty.

choices.why: The phrase is David's stated reason for sparing Saul; rendering as 'anointed' preserves the Hebrew sense of mashiach that Chrysostom is invoking, rather than reading it as a proper name for Jesus.
The phrase means 'with ample margin' or 'superabundantly'; keeping the literal 'abundance' preserves Chrysostom's rhetorical emphasis on the excess of evidence.
The term refers to the innermost sacred space; 'sanctuaries' conveys the forbidden holy precincts of the priesthood without importing temple-specific vocabulary.
The metaphor is of a handle by which someone might seize or accuse; 'handle' preserves the concrete image.
The verb πλύνειν means 'to wash' and is used metaphorically for drenching someone in abuse; keeping 'wash' preserves the vivid image.
The term refers to the sacred rites, especially the Eucharist; 'mysteries' is the standard English term for the sacramental rites in patristic usage.

pass_b_english: For this reason David, when he had Saul in his power—Saul who was acting lawlessly, breathing murder, and deserving of countless punishments—not only spared his life, but would not even utter a harsh word against him. And he gives the reason when he says, 'He is the Lord's anointed' (1 Samuel 24:6). And not only from this, but from another example as well, you can see from great abundance how far the one under authority must stand from correcting the affairs of priests. For once, when the ark was being brought up, some of those under authority saw it tilting and about to fall, and set it upright—and they paid the penalty on the spot, struck by the Lord and left dead. And yet they were doing nothing improper: they were not overturning the ark, but setting upright what was about to topple and fall. But so that you might learn from great abundance the dignity of priests, and how it is not lawful for one who is subject and in the rank of the laity to correct such things, he killed them in the midst of the crowd, striking fear into all the rest by the great excess of it, and persuading them never to approach the sacred precincts of the priesthood. For if each person were going to bring himself into the dignity of the priesthood on the pretext of correcting what is done badly, neither would a pretext for correction ever be lacking, nor would we be able to distinguish ruler from ruled, since everything would be mixed together.

And let no one think that I say these things because I have condemned the priests—for by the grace of God they display great gentleness in all things, as you yourselves know, and have never given anyone any handle—but so that you may learn that even if you had wicked fathers and burdensome teachers, it would not be safe or secure for you even then to slander and revile them. For if concerning bodily parents a wise man says, 'Even if he loses understanding, forgive him; for what will you give back to them, as they have given to you?' (Sirach 3:13; 7:28), much more must this law be kept concerning spiritual parents, and each person must busy himself with and examine his own life, so that we do not hear on that day, 'Hypocrite, why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?' (Matthew 7:3).

For it is the work of hypocrites to kiss the hands of priests in public where everyone can see, and to touch their knees, and to ask them to pray on their behalf, and to run to their doors when in need of baptism—but at home and in the marketplaces to deluge with countless reproaches those who are the cause and ministers of so many good things for us, or to tolerate others who reproach them. For if the father is truly wicked, how do you consider him a trustworthy minister of those awesome mysteries? But if he seems to you a trustworthy minister of those things, why do you tolerate others speaking evil of him, and do not silence them, or grow indignant, or show displeasure, so that you may receive a great reward from God, and praise from those very accusers? For even if they are insolent ten thousand times over, they will certainly praise you and approve your care for your fathers; just as, if we do not do this, everyone will condemn us—even those who speak evil themselves. And this is not the only terrible thing, but also that we will pay the ultimate penalty there.

problems.why: 'Syngnōmēn eche' means 'have forgiveness/pardon' or 'excuse him,' not merely patience; the sense is pardon/excuse.
problems.ruling: συγγνώμην ἔχε means 'have forgiveness/pardon,' not patience; meaning is changed.

fixed: Changed 'have patience' to 'forgive him' for 'συγγνώμην ἔχε', which means 'have pardon/forgiveness', not merely patience.

problems.why: ἄδυτον means 'inner sanctuary, holy of holies, inaccessible place'—the sacred/inner precincts of priesthood, not 'sanctuaries' generally. 'Sanctuaries' is too broad and loses the sense of forbidden/inaccessible sacred space.
problems.fix: the sacred precincts of the priesthood

last_rejected.quote: he killed them in the midst of the crowd
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀπέκτεινεν αὐτοὺς ἐν μέσῳ τῷ πλήθει
last_rejected.why: The subject of 'ἀπέκτεινεν' is God/the Lord (ὑπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου πληγέντες καὶ νεκροὶ μείναντες earlier, and the context is divine punishment). The English 'he killed them' makes it sound like David or an unspecified human agent, but it refers to God's action. The Greek has passive 'struck by the Lord' then active 'killed them' with God as implied subject. The English 'he' is ambiguous and could mislead.
last_rejected.fix: the Lord killed them in the midst of the crowd
last_rejected.ruling: Context makes clear God killed them; 'he' is standard pronominal reference, not misleading.

last_rejected.why: 'ἄδυτα' means 'inner sanctuaries, adyta, holy of holies, inaccessible places' - the most sacred inner chambers. 'Sacred precincts' is too weak and general; it loses the sense of restricted, forbidden access that makes the punishment's severity comprehensible. The word carries the meaning of 'inaccessible/innermost sanctuary.'
last_rejected.ruling: 'Sacred precincts' is within normal range for ἄδυτα; not a meaning change or loss.

last_rejected.why: 'πλύνειν' with 'ὀνείδεσι' is a vivid metaphor - 'to wash with reproaches' means 'to drench, flood, overwhelm with reproaches.' But 'wash' in English suggests cleansing, which is opposite of the sense. The metaphor is 'to drench/flood someone with abuse.' 'Wash' is a false friend or misleading rendering.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Wash with reproaches' preserves the metaphor; English readers understand drenching, not cleansing.

last_rejected.quote: or to tolerate others who reproach them
last_rejected.why: The English 'or to tolerate others who reproach them' is present. Wait, let me re-check. Actually it is there. Let me look more carefully. The phrase 'ἢ ἑτέρων ὀνειδιζόντων ἀνέχεσθαι' = 'or to endure others reproaching them.' The English has 'or to tolerate others who reproach them.' This is present. No omission.
last_rejected.ruling: No omission; English 'or to tolerate others who reproach them' renders the Greek phrase.

last_rejected.why: 'δυσχεραίνεις' means 'to be vexed, annoyed, indignant, take it ill' - 'show displeasure' is rather weak and polite. The word carries stronger emotion of being upset/angered by something. 'Grow indignant' was used for 'ἀγανακτεῖς' just before, but 'δυσχεραίνειν' is similar or stronger.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Show displeasure' is within normal range for δυσχεραίνειν; mere preference for stronger wording.
